checks.title: The price of mutation is e^−U
checks.why: Haldane (1937) and Muller (1950): at balance every new damaging mutation is removed by one death or failed birth, so with U = 1 new mutation per newborn the share of young that survive their genes settles at e^−1 = 36.8 %.
checks.source: Haldane 1937, Am. Nat. 71:337; Muller 1950, Am. J. Hum. Genet. 2:111

checks.title: The price does not depend on how harmful each gene is
checks.why: Ten times milder genes, same share of young lost: a milder mutation lingers longer and so is carried by more of the young before it is removed, and the two effects cancel. (Wright’s distribution, which adds drift, gives 37.8 %.)

checks.title: Broken copies per genome: U/(h·s)
checks.why: Each broken copy lowers survival by h·s = 1.25 % and so lasts about 1/(h·s) = 80 generations. With one new one per newborn per generation, a genome carries about 80. (Drift trims this a little; Wright’s distribution gives 78.)

checks.title: Milder genes: more broken copies, as Wright predicts
checks.why: U/(h·s) would give 800, but at s = 0.5 % drift starts to matter (4N·h·s = 10): by chance some genes are clean in everyone for a while. Wright’s stationary distribution for mutation, selection and drift gives 684.

checks.title: More dominant damage: fewer broken copies, same price
checks.why: With h = 0.5 a single broken copy costs twice as much, so it is removed twice as fast: U/(h·s) = 40 copies. The price stays e^−U.

checks.title: Enough young to pay the price, or extinction
checks.simulated: U = 2 died out after 163 generations; U = 1.2 lived (survival 30.4 %)
checks.why: Each female has F = 10 young, so at least 2 in 10 must survive for the population to replace itself. With U = 2 only e^−2 = 13.5 % survive at balance; with U = 1.2, 30 %.

checks.title: Genes nobody needs decay at the mutation rate
runs: Genes that do not matter (s = 0.0001 %), 500 places
checks.why: With no selection, broken copies just pile up: each intact copy breaks at rate u = 1/10,240 per generation (and is repaired ten times more rarely), so after 5,000 generations 37.8 % of copies are broken, heading for 91 %. This is how pseudogenes form.

checks.title: Neutral substitution rate = mutation rate
runs: Genes that do not matter, rare mutations (U = 0.05), 500 places
checks.detail: genes broken in every copy, generations 5,000 to 35,000
checks.why: Kimura: a new neutral mutation takes over with chance 1/(2N), and 2N·u of them arise each generation, so neutral genes turn over at rate u, whatever the population size.

checks.title: Slightly harmful mutations take over too, more rarely
runs: Slightly harmful genes (s = 0.2 %, h = 0.5), rare mutations, 500 places
checks.detail: Kimura’s chance of taking over: 0.31 × the neutral one (4N·h·s = 2)
checks.why: When 4N·h·s is near 1, drift can carry a harmful mutation all the way: Kimura’s fixation probability gives about a third of the neutral rate here. This is how small populations collect damage.

checks.title: Without sex the best genomes are lost for good
runs: Clones: severe genes, U = 0.1, no sex
checks.predicted: the clones’ fewest broken copies climbs; with sex it stays near 0 (Haigh: 0.67 genomes in the best class)
checks.simulated: clones: fewest 3 → 54, survival 47.8 %; sex: fewest 1 → 0, survival 89.7 %
checks.tolerance: clones gain at least 20, sex ends at 3 or fewer
checks.why: Muller’s ratchet: in clones the least damaged genomes, only about N·e^−U/(h·s) of them, are lost by chance and cannot be rebuilt except by rare repairs. With sex, recombination keeps making clean genomes from damaged parents.
checks.source: Muller 1964, Mutat. Res. 1:2; Felsenstein 1974, Genetics 78:737; Haigh 1978

checks.title: Damage that hurts more and more lowers the price
runs: Severe genes, damage that hurts more and more (synergy 2)
checks.why: With synergy each death removes more broken copies than average, so fewer deaths are needed: Kimura & Maruyama’s balance for a Poisson number of mutations gives 46.9 %, above e^−U = 36.8 %.
checks.source: Kimura & Maruyama 1966; Kondrashov 1988; Charlesworth 1990, Genet. Res. 55:199

checks.title: Selection on males lowers the price to e^−{U/(1 + m/2)}
runs: Severe genes, healthier males father more young (selection on males 2)
checks.detail: broken copies per genome 39.5, predicted U/(h·s·(1 + m/2)) = 40.0
checks.why: With m = 2 a male’s damage costs him twice as much in matings as in survival. A broken copy then leaves the population through its male carriers’ lost matings as well as through deaths, so balance needs only half as many broken copies and the young pay only half the deaths: e^−0.5 = 60.7 % survive instead of 36.8 %. The lost matings cost nothing, because other males father those young.
checks.source: Agrawal 2001, Nature 411:692; Siller 2001, Nature 411:689; Whitlock & Agrawal 2009, Evolution 63:569

checks.title: The default genome after a million years: Wright’s forecast
runs: The default population, one million years (40,000 generations)
checks.detail: broken copies per genome by effect, simulated (forecast): severe 38 (39), mild 367 (376), slight 1,326 (1,411), tiny 2,868 (2,898)
checks.why: Summing Wright’s distribution over all 5,120 genes forecasts the long-run genome: severe genes stay almost clean, while genes too weak for selection to see (4N·h·s below 1) end up mostly broken. After 40,000 generations the simulation is within a few percent of it.

checks.title: … and the share of young that survive it
runs: The default population, one million years (40,000 generations)
checks.why: The load now has two parts: about U from genes under selection, plus the cost of weak genes that drift has broken in everyone. Forecast and simulation agree, and the population stays above the 20 % it needs.
checks.source: Kimura, Maruyama & Crow 1963; Lynch, Conery & Bürger 1995, Am. Nat. 146:489

checks.title: Same seed, same run
runs: The default population twice with one seed, once with another (500 generations)
checks.detail: fingerprints of every genome after 500 generations
checks.why: Every random draw comes from one seeded generator, so a run can be repeated exactly, here, in Node or in CI.
